Critical regularity issues for the compressible Navier–Stokes system in bounded domains

Raphaël Danchin and Patrick Tolksdorf Address: Université Paris-Est, LAMA, UMR 8050, 61 Avenue du Général de Gaulle, 94010 Créteil, Cedex, France Address: Institut für Mathematik, Johannes Gutenberg-Universität Mainz, Staudingerweg 9, 55099 Mainz, Germany Email address: danchin@univ-paris12.fr Email address: tolksdorf@uni-mainz.de
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We are concerned with the barotropic compressible Navier–Stokes system in a bounded domain of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} (with d≥2d\geq 2). In a critical regularity setting, we establish local well-posedness for large data with no vacuum and global well-posedness for small perturbations of a stable constant equilibrium state.

Our results rely on new maximal regularity estimates - of independent interest - for the semigroup of the Lamé operator, and of the linearized compressible Navier–Stokes equations.

1. Introduction

We are concerned with the following barotropic compressible Navier–Stokes system in a 𝒞∞\mathcal{C}^{\infty} bounded domain Ω\Omega of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, d≥2d\geq 2:

(1.1) {∂tρ+div⁡(ρ​u)=0in ​ℝ+×Ω,∂t(ρ​u)+div⁡(ρ​u⊗u)−2​div⁡(μ​D​(u))−∇(λ​div⁡u)+∇P=0in ​ℝ+×Ω,u=0on ​ℝ+×∂Ω,(ρ,u)|t=0=(ρ0,u0)in ​Ω.\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}\rho+\divergence(\rho u)=0\quad&\hbox{in }\ \mathbb{R}_{+}\times\Omega,\\ &\partial_{t}(\rho u)+\divergence(\rho u\otimes u)-2\divergence(\mu D(u))-\nabla(\lambda\divergence u)+\nabla P=0&\quad\hbox{in }\ \mathbb{R}_{+}\times\Omega,\\ &u=0&\quad\hbox{on }\ \mathbb{R}_{+}\times\partial\Omega,\\ &(\rho,u)|_{t=0}=(\rho_{0},u_{0})&\quad\hbox{in }\ \Omega.\end{aligned}\right.

The unknowns are the (scalar nonnegative) density ρ=ρ⁡(t,x)\rho=\rho(t,x) and the vector-field u=u⁡(t,x).u=u(t,x). The notation D⁡(u)D(u) stands for the symmetric part of the Jacobian matrix of u.u. The viscosity coefficients λ\lambda and μ\mu are smooth functions of ρ\rho satisfying μ>0\mu>0 and λ+2​μ>0.\lambda+2\mu>0. We shall often assume (with no loss of generality) that the average value of the density on Ω,\Omega, a conserved quantity, is equal to 1.1.

The mathematical study of the Cauchy problem (or initial boundary value problem) for the compressible Navier–Stokes system has been initiated sixty years ago with the pioneering works by J. Serrin [32] and J. Nash [31] who established the local-in-time existence and uniqueness of classical solutions. In the case Ω=ℝ3,\Omega=\mathbb{R}^{3}, the global existence of strong solutions with Sobolev regularity has been first proved by A. Matsumura and T. Nishida [25], for small perturbations of a constant state (ρ,u)=(ρ¯,0)(\rho,u)=(\bar{\rho},0) under the stability condition P′​(ρ¯)>0.P^{\prime}(\bar{\rho})>0. The proof was based on subtle energy estimates that enabled the authors to pinpoint some L2\mathrm{L}^{2}-in-time integrability for both the density and the velocity, as well as algebraic time decay estimates.

With completely different methods based on parabolic maximal regularity in the framework of Lebesgue spaces, local existence has been established by V. Solonnikov [33] for general data with no vacuum (see also the more recent work by the first author [8] where critical regularity is almost achieved) as well as global existence for small perturbations of (ρ¯,0)(\bar{\rho},0) (see  [29], and [21]).

In the present paper, we want to recover the classical results of strong solutions for (1.1) in the bounded domain case within a critical regularity setting, that is, in functional spaces that are invariant by the following rescaling for all ℓ>0\ell>0:

(1.2) (ρ0(x),u0(x))↝(ρ0(ℓx),ℓu0(ℓx))and(ρ(t,x),u(t,x))↝(ρ(ℓ2t,ℓx),ℓu(ℓ2t,ℓx))⋅\bigl(\rho_{0}(x),u_{0}(x)\bigr)\leadsto\bigl(\rho_{0}(\ell x),\ell u_{0}(\ell x)\bigr)\quad\hbox{and}\quad\bigl(\rho(t,x),u(t,x)\bigr)\leadsto\bigl(\rho(\ell^{2}t,\ell x),\ell u(\ell^{2}t,\ell x)\bigr)\cdotp

Observe that the above rescaling leaves the whole system invariant, up to a change of the pressure term (provided the fluid domain is dilated accordingly, of course). As first noticed by H. Fujita and T. Kato in [17] for the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations, working in scaling invariant spaces is the key to getting optimal well-posedness results.

Our main goal here is to prove the following type of statements:

  • •

    local well-posedness for general data having critical regularity and such that ρ0>0\rho_{0}>0;

  • •

    if, in addition, P′​(1)>0,P^{\prime}(1)>0, global well-posedness for data (ρ0,u0)(\rho_{0},u_{0}) that are small perturbations of (1,0)(1,0) (for some norm having the invariance of the first part of (1.2)).

When the fluid domain is the whole space, a number of results in that spirit have been established, and the critical norms are always built upon homogeneous Besov spaces with last index equal to 11. More precisely, it has been first observed in [7] that one can take any data such that ρ0−1\rho_{0}-1 is small in B˙2,1d/2−1​(ℝd)∩B˙2,1d/2​(ℝd),\dot{\mathrm{B}}^{d/2-1}_{2,1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap\dot{\mathrm{B}}^{d/2}_{2,1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), and u0u_{0} is small in B˙2,1d/2−1​(ℝd).\dot{\mathrm{B}}^{d/2-1}_{2,1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Later works (see, e.g., [5], [6]) pointed out that it is actually enough to assume the high frequencies of the data to be in the larger space B˙p,1d/p​(ℝd)×B˙p,1d/p−1​(ℝd)\dot{\mathrm{B}}^{d/p}_{p,1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\times\dot{\mathrm{B}}^{d/p-1}_{p,1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) for some pp in the range (2,min(4,2​dd−2))⋅\bigl(2,\min(4,\frac{2d}{d-2})\bigr)\cdotp

Here we aim at extending those results to the physically relevant case where the fluid domain is bounded and the velocity vanishes at the boundary. Compared to works in the whole space, the expected difficulty is that one can no longer use techniques based on the Fourier transform to investigate (1.1) (in particular, global results of [7] were based on a decomposition into low and high frequencies of the solution). Whether one can adapt those techniques to the domain case is unclear. In the present paper, we focus on the bounded domain case which is expected to be easier than the unbounded domain case since, somehow, low frequencies do not exist (therefore, prescribing different regularity for low and high frequencies is irrelevant).

Since the linearized compressible Navier–Stokes system may be associated to an analytic semigroup in suitable functional spaces, using maximal Lq\mathrm{L}^{q}-regularity seems to be an acceptable substitute to Fourier analysis. However, as already pointed out in previous works (see, e.g., [8]), reaching critical regularity within the classical theory would require maximal L1\mathrm{L}^{1}-regularity, which is false in the setting of Lebesgue or Sobolev spaces for instance.

For the reader’s convenience, let us briefly recall what maximal regularity is. Let XX be a Banach space and −A:𝒟⁡(A)⊂X→X,-A:\mathcal{D}(A)\subset X\to X, the generator of a bounded analytic semigroup (T⁡(t))t≥0(T(t))_{t\geq 0} on X.X. Consider for f∈Lq​(ℝ+,X)f\in\mathrm{L}^{q}(\mathbb{R}_{+};X), 1≤q≤∞1\leq q\leq\infty, the abstract Cauchy problem

{u′​(t)+A​u​(t)=f(t)(t>0),u⁡(0)=0.\displaystyle\left\{\begin{aligned} u^{\prime}(t)+Au(t)&=f(t)\qquad(t>0),\\ u(0)&=0.\end{aligned}\right.

By virtue of [4, Prop. 3.1.16] the unique mild solution to this problem is given by the variation of constants formula

u⁡(t)=∫0tT⁡(t−τ)​f​(τ)​𝑑τ(t>0).\displaystyle u(t)=\int_{0}^{t}T(t-\tau)f(\tau)\;\mathrm{d}\tau\qquad(t>0).

We say that AA has maximal Lq\mathrm{L}^{q}-regularity if, for every f∈Lq​(ℝ+,X),f\in\mathrm{L}^{q}(\mathbb{R}_{+};X), it holds for almost every t>0t>0 that u⁡(t)∈𝒟⁡(A),u(t)\in\mathcal{D}(A), and A​u∈Lq​(ℝ+,X)Au\in\mathrm{L}^{q}(\mathbb{R}_{+};X). Notice that in this case also u′∈Lq​(ℝ+,X)u^{\prime}\in\mathrm{L}^{q}(\mathbb{R}_{+};X) and that the closed graph theorem implies the existence of a constant C>0C>0 such that for all f∈Lq​(ℝ+,X)f\in\mathrm{L}^{q}(\mathbb{R}_{+};X) it holds

∥u′,Au∥Lq​(ℝ+,X)≤C∥f∥Lq​(ℝ+,X).\displaystyle\|u^{\prime},Au\|_{\mathrm{L}^{q}(\mathbb{R}_{+};X)}\leq C\|f\|_{\mathrm{L}^{q}(\mathbb{R}_{+};X)}.

See the monographs of Denk, Hieber, and Prüss [13] and of Kunstmann and Weis [23] for further information. Our aim here is to adapt an argument of real interpolation that originates from Da Prato-Grisvard’s work in [12] so as to reach the endpoint q=1q=1 that turns out to be the key to proving global-in-time results in critical regularity framework (in this respect, see also our recent paper [11]).

We perform the analysis first for the semigroup associated to the Lamé operator (namely the linearization of the velocity equation if neglecting the pressure term), so as to get a local well-posedness result for general data with critical regularity, then for the linearization of the whole system (1.1) about (ρ,u)=(1,0)(\rho,u)=(1,0) to obtain a global result.

Back to the nonlinear system, one cannot just push all nonlinear terms to the right-hand side and bound them according to Duhamel’s formula, though. The troublemaker is the convection term in the density equation, namely u⋅∇ρ,u\cdot\nabla\rho, that causes a loss of one derivative (this reflects the fact that the system under consideration is partly hyperbolic). The way to overcome the difficulty is well-known: it is called Lagrangian coordinates. Indeed, if rewriting (1.1) in Lagrangian coordinates, then one just has to consider the evolution equation for the velocity which is of parabolic type. Therefore, not only the loss of derivative may be avoided, but also the solution may be obtained (either locally for large data, or globally for small data) by means of the contraction mapping argument in Banach spaces.

Let us now come to the main results of the paper.

Theorem 1.1.

Assume that Ω\Omega is a smooth bounded domain of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} (d≥2d\geq 2) and let pp be in (d−1,2​d).(d-1,2d). Then, for all initial densities ρ0∈Bp,1d/p​(Ω),\rho_{0}\in\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}(\Omega), positive and bounded away from zero, and all u0∈Bp,1d/p−1​(Ω,ℝd),u_{0}\in\mathrm{B}^{d/p-1}_{p,1}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{d}), System (1.1) admits a unique solution (ρ,u)(\rho,u) on some nontrivial time interval [0,T],[0,T], such that (ρ,u)∈𝒞b​([0,T],Bp,1d/p​(Ω)×Bp,1d/p−1​(Ω,ℝd))(\rho,u)\in\mathcal{C}_{b}([0,T];\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}(\Omega)\times\mathrm{B}^{d/p-1}_{p,1}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{d})) and

(ρ,u)∈W1,1(ℝ+;Bp,1d/p(Ω)×Bp,1d/p−1(Ω;ℝd))∩L1(ℝ+;Bp,1d/p(Ω)×Bp,1d/p+1(Ω;ℝd))⋅(\rho,u)\in\mathrm{W}^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}_{+};\mathrm{B}^{{d}/{p}}_{p,1}(\Omega)\times\mathrm{B}^{{d}/{p}-1}_{p,1}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{d}))\cap\mathrm{L}^{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+};\mathrm{B}^{{d}/{p}}_{p,1}(\Omega)\times\mathrm{B}^{{d}/{p}+1}_{p,1}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{d}))\cdotp

Furthermore, inf(t,x)∈[0,T]×Ωρ⁡(t,x)>0\inf_{(t,x)\in[0,T]\times\Omega}\>\rho(t,x)>0 and the average of ρ\rho is time independent.

Proving a global result for small perturbations of a stable constant state is based on maximal regularity estimates for the linearized compressible Navier–Stokes system (where μ′=λ+μ\mu^{\prime}=\lambda+\mu):

(1.3) {∂ta+div⁡u=fin ​ℝ+×Ω,∂tu−μΔu−μ′∇divu+∇a=gin ​ℝ+×Ω,u=0on ​ℝ+×∂Ω,(a,u)|t=0=(a0,u0)in ​Ω.\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}a+\divergence u=f\quad&\hbox{in }\ \mathbb{R}_{+}\times\Omega,\\ &\partial_{t}u-\mu\Delta u-\mu^{\prime}\nabla\divergence u+\nabla a=g&\quad\hbox{in }\ \mathbb{R}_{+}\times\Omega,\\ &u=0&\quad\hbox{on }\ \mathbb{R}_{+}\times\partial\Omega,\\ &(a,u)|_{t=0}=(a_{0},u_{0})&\quad\hbox{in }\ \Omega.\end{aligned}\right.

The following statement extends the work by P.B. Mucha and W. Zaja̧czkowski [29] to the endpoint case where the time Lebesgue exponent is equal to 1,1, and also provides exponential decay for the solutions of the system.

Theorem 1.2.

Take initial data (a0,u0)(a_{0},u_{0}) in Bp,1s+1​(Ω)×Bp,1s​(Ω,ℝd)\mathrm{B}^{s+1}_{p,1}(\Omega)\times\mathrm{B}^{s}_{p,1}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{d}) and source terms (f,g)(f,g) in L1​(ℝ+,Bp,1s+1​(Ω)×Bp,1s​(Ω,ℝd))\mathrm{L}^{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+};\mathrm{B}^{s+1}_{p,1}(\Omega)\times\mathrm{B}^{s}_{p,1}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{d})) with (s,p)(s,p) satisfying

1<p<∞andmax(1p,dp−d2)−1<s<1p⋅1<p<\infty\quad\hbox{and}\quad\max\biggl(\frac{1}{p},\frac{d}{p}-\frac{d}{2}\biggr)-1<s<\frac{1}{p}\cdotp

Assume also that the average of a0a_{0} and of f⁡(t)f(t) (for a.e. t>0t>0) is zero. Then, System (1.3) has a unique global solution (a,u)(a,u) in the space

(1.4) Eps:=W1,1(ℝ+;Bp,1s+1(Ω)×Bp,1s(Ω;ℝd))∩L1(ℝ+;Bp,1s+1(Ω)×Bp,1s+2(Ω;ℝd))⋅\displaystyle\mathrm{E}_{p}^{s}:=\mathrm{W}^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}_{+};\mathrm{B}^{s+1}_{p,1}(\Omega)\times\mathrm{B}^{s}_{p,1}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{d}))\cap\mathrm{L}^{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+};\mathrm{B}^{s+1}_{p,1}(\Omega)\times\mathrm{B}^{s+2}_{p,1}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{d}))\cdotp

Additionally, there exist two positive constants cc and CC depending only on p,p, Ω,\Omega, μ\mu, and μ′\mu^{\prime} such that if ec​t​(f,g)∈L1​(ℝ+,Bp,1s+1​(Ω)×Bp,1s​(Ω,ℝd))\mathrm{e}^{ct}(f,g)\in\mathrm{L}^{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+};\mathrm{B}^{s+1}_{p,1}(\Omega)\times\mathrm{B}^{s}_{p,1}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{d})), then

(1.5) ∥ec​t(a,u)∥Eps≤C(∥(a0,u0)∥Bp,1s+1×Bp,1s+∥ec​t(f,g)∥L1​(ℝ+,Bp,1s+1×Bp,1s))⋅\|\mathrm{e}^{ct}(a,u)\|_{\mathrm{E}^{s}_{p}}\leq C\biggl(\|(a_{0},u_{0})\|_{\mathrm{B}^{s+1}_{p,1}\times\mathrm{B}^{s}_{p,1}}+\|\mathrm{e}^{ct}(f,g)\|_{\mathrm{L}^{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+};\mathrm{B}^{s+1}_{p,1}\times\mathrm{B}^{s}_{p,1})}\biggr)\cdotp

After recasting System (1.1) in Lagrangian coordinates, combining the above result with nonlinear estimates allows to get the following global well-posedness result for critical regularity:

Theorem 1.3.

Let Ω,\Omega, pp, and dd be as in Theorem 1.1 and assume in addition that P′​(1)>0.P^{\prime}(1)>0. Let ρ0∈Bp,1d/p​(Ω)\rho_{0}\in\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}(\Omega) with average 11 and u0∈Bp,1d/p−1​(Ω,ℝd).u_{0}\in\mathrm{B}^{d/p-1}_{p,1}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{d}). There exists a constant α=α⁡(λ,μ,p,d,P,Ω)>0\alpha=\alpha(\lambda,\mu,p,d,P,\Omega)>0 such that if a0:=ρ0−1a_{0}:=\rho_{0}-1 and u0u_{0} satisfy

(1.6) ‖a0‖Bp,1d/p+‖u0‖Bp,1d/p−1≤α,\|a_{0}\|_{\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}}+\|u_{0}\|_{\mathrm{B}^{d/p-1}_{p,1}}\leq\alpha,

then System (1.1) admits a unique global solution (ρ,u)(\rho,u) with (a,u):=(ρ−1,u)(a,u):=(\rho-1,u) in the maximal regularity space Ep:=Epd/p−1.\mathrm{E}_{p}:=\mathrm{E}_{p}^{d/p-1}. In addition, there exists c>0c>0 depending only on the parameters of the system, on pp, and on Ω\Omega such that (a,u)(a,u) fulfills:

∥ec​t(a,u)∥Ep≤C(∥a0∥Bp,1d/p+∥u0∥Bp,1d/p−1)⋅\|\mathrm{e}^{ct}(a,u)\|_{\mathrm{E}_{p}}\leq C\bigl(\|a_{0}\|_{\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}}+\|u_{0}\|_{\mathrm{B}^{d/p-1}_{p,1}}\bigr)\cdotp

The rest of the paper unfolds as follows. The next two sections are dedicated to the “linear study” namely proving maximal regularity results first for the Lamé operator, and next for the linearized compressible Navier–Stokes system. In Section 5, we prove our main global existence result. In Section 6, we establish local existence results with no smallness condition on the velocity, first in the easy case where the initial density is close to a constant and, next, assuming only that the density is bounded away from zero. Some technical results are recalled/proved in Appendix.

2. Some background from semigroup theory

We use this section to introduce the basic functional analytic notions and arguments that are crucial for the theory that is developed afterwards.

Let XX denote a Banach space over the complex field. For θ∈(0,π)\theta\in(0,\pi) define the sector Sθ\mathrm{S}_{\theta} in the complex plane

Sθ:={z∈ℂ∖{0}:|arg⁡(z)|<θ},\displaystyle\mathrm{S}_{\theta}:=\{z\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}:\lvert\arg(z)\rvert<\theta\},

and set S0:=(0,∞)\mathrm{S}_{0}:=(0,\infty).

The standard definition of (bounded) analytic semigroups reads:

Definition 2.1.

A family (T⁡(z))z∈Sθ∪{0}⊂ℒ⁡(X)(T(z))_{z\in\mathrm{S}_{\theta}\cup\{0\}}\subset{\mathcal{L}}(X), θ∈(0,π/2]\theta\in(0,\pi/2], is called an analytic semigroup of angle θ\theta if

  1. (1)

    T⁡(0)=IdT(0)=\Id and T⁡(z+w)=T⁡(z)​T​(w)T(z+w)=T(z)T(w) for all z,w∈Sθz,w\in\mathrm{S}_{\theta};

  2. (2)

    the map z↦T⁡(z)z\mapsto T(z) is analytic in Sθ\mathrm{S}_{\theta};

  3. (3)

    limSϑ∋z→0T⁡(z)​x=x\lim_{\mathrm{S}_{\vartheta}\ni z\to 0}T(z)x=x for all x∈Xx\in X and all 0<ϑ<θ0<\vartheta<\theta.

If in addition

  1. (4)

    ‖T⁡(z)‖ℒ⁡(X)\|T(z)\|_{{\mathcal{L}}(X)} is bounded in Sϑ\mathrm{S}_{\vartheta} for all 0<ϑ<θ0<\vartheta<\theta,

the family (T⁡(z))z∈Sθ∪{0}(T(z))_{z\in\mathrm{S}_{\theta}\cup\{0\}} is called a bounded analytic semigroup.

To any analytic semigroup of some angle θ∈(0,π/2],\theta\in(0,\pi/2], one can attach a unique operator A:𝒟⁡(A)⊂X→XA:\mathcal{D}(A)\subset X\to X defined by

𝒟⁡(A):={x∈X:limt→01t​(T⁡(t)​x−x)​ exists}\displaystyle\mathcal{D}(A):=\Big\{x\in X:\lim_{t\to 0}\frac{1}{t}(T(t)x-x)\text{ exists}\Big\}

and, for x∈𝒟⁡(A),x\in\mathcal{D}(A),

Ax:=−limt→01t(T(t)x−x).\displaystyle Ax:=-\lim_{t\to 0}\frac{1}{t}(T(t)x-x).

The operator −A-A is called the generator of (T⁡(z))z∈Sθ∪{0}.(T(z))_{z\in\mathrm{S}_{\theta}\cup\{0\}}.

Combining (1) and (2) one readily sees that the range of T⁡(z)T(z) is contained in 𝒟⁡(A)\mathcal{D}(A) for any z∈Sθz\in\mathrm{S}_{\theta} and that the function u:[0,∞)→Xu:[0,\infty)\to X given by u⁡(t):=T⁡(t)​xu(t):=T(t)x solves the abstract Cauchy problem

(2.1) {u′​(t)+A​u​(t)=0t>0,u⁡(0)=x.\displaystyle\left\{\begin{aligned} u^{\prime}(t)+Au(t)&=0&&t>0,\\ u(0)&=x.\end{aligned}\right.

From the PDE perspective, one can wonder if, whenever A:𝒟⁡(A)⊂X→XA:\mathcal{D}(A)\subset X\to X is a given linear operator, −A-A is the generator of an analytic semigroup. At this point, we need to recall the notion of a sectorial operator.

Definition 2.2.

A linear operator B:𝒟⁡(B)⊂X→XB:\mathcal{D}(B)\subset X\to X is called sectorial of angle ω\omega for some ω∈[0,π)\omega\in[0,\pi) if its spectrum satisfies σ⁡(B)⊂Sω¯\sigma(B)\subset\overline{\mathrm{S}_{\omega}} and if for all ω<ω′<π\omega<\omega^{\prime}<\pi there exists C>0C>0 such that

‖λ​(λ−B)−1‖ℒ⁡(X)≤C(λ∈ℂ∖Sω′¯).\displaystyle\|\lambda(\lambda-B)^{-1}\|_{{\mathcal{L}}(X)}\leq C\qquad(\lambda\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\overline{\mathrm{S}_{\omega^{\prime}}}).

The following characterization theorem for analytic semigroups is classical [15, Thm. II.4.6].

Theorem 2.3.

Let A:𝒟⁡(A)⊂X→XA:\mathcal{D}(A)\subset X\to X be a linear operator. Then −A-A is the generator of an analytic semigroup if and only if AA is densely defined and there exists z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C} such that z+Az+A is sectorial of some angle ω∈[0,π/2)\omega\in[0,\pi/2). Moreover, −A-A generates a bounded analytic semigroup if and only if additionally one can choose z=0z=0, i.e., AA itself is sectorial of angle ω∈[0,π/2)\omega\in[0,\pi/2).

Remark 2.4.

The condition that z+Az+A is sectorial of angle ω∈[0,π/2)\omega\in[0,\pi/2) is equivalent to the fact that there exists R>0R>0 such that σ⁡(−A)⊂Sω¯∪B⁡(0,R)\sigma(-A)\subset\overline{\mathrm{S}_{\omega}}\cup B(0,R) and such that

‖λ​(λ+A)−1‖ℒ⁡(X)≤C(λ∈ℂ∖[Sω′¯∪B⁡(0,R)]).\displaystyle\|\lambda(\lambda+A)^{-1}\|_{{\mathcal{L}}(X)}\leq C\qquad(\lambda\in\mathbb{C}\setminus[\overline{\mathrm{S}_{\omega^{\prime}}}\cup B(0,R)]).
Remark 2.5.

If −A-A generates a bounded analytic semigroup and if 0∈ρ⁡(A)0\in\rho(A), then the corresponding semigroup is exponentially decaying. Indeed, as AA is sectorial of angle ω∈[0,π/2)\omega\in[0,\pi/2) and as the resolvent set is open, one finds that

infλ∈σ⁡(A)Re⁡(λ)>0.\displaystyle\inf_{\lambda\in\sigma(A)}\operatorname{Re}(\lambda)>0.

Thus, there exists ε>0\varepsilon>0 and ω′∈[0,π/2)\omega^{\prime}\in[0,\pi/2) such that A−εA-\varepsilon is sectorial of angle ω′\omega^{\prime} which implies that the semigroup generated by ε−A\varepsilon-A is bounded. This in turn implies the exponential decay of the semigroup generated by −A-A.

To solve nonlinear equations, it is helpful to consider (2.1) for a homogeneous initial value but for an inhomogeneous right-hand side of the first equation, i.e.,

(2.2) {u′​(t)+A​u​(t)=f⁡(t)t∈(0,T),u⁡(0)=0,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{aligned} u^{\prime}(t)+Au(t)&=f(t)&&t\in(0,T),\\ u(0)&=0,\end{aligned}\right.

where 0<T≤∞0<T\leq\infty and f∈Lq​(0,T,X)f\in\mathrm{L}^{q}(0,T;X), 1≤q≤∞1\leq q\leq\infty. As recalled in the introduction, a densely defined operator A:𝒟⁡(A)⊂X→XA:\mathcal{D}(A)\subset X\to X is said to have maximal Lq\mathrm{L}^{q}-regularity if there exists a constant C>0C>0 such that for all f∈Lq​(0,T,X),f\in\mathrm{L}^{q}(0,T;X), System (2.2) has a unique solution uu that satisfies u⁡(t)∈𝒟⁡(A)u(t)\in\mathcal{D}(A) for almost all t∈(0,T),t\in(0,T), is almost everywhere differentiable and such that

∥u′,Au∥Lq​(0,T,X)≤C∥f∥Lq​(0,T,X).\displaystyle\|u^{\prime},Au\|_{\mathrm{L}^{q}(0,T;X)}\leq C\|f\|_{\mathrm{L}^{q}(0,T;X)}.

It is classical, see, e.g., Dore [14, Cor. 4.4], that the maximal Lq\mathrm{L}^{q}-regularity of AA implies that −A-A generates an analytic semigroup. Characterizing when a given operator admits maximal Lq\mathrm{L}^{q}-regularity is often a difficult issue, which involves questions on the geometry of Banach spaces and operator-valued multiplier theorems, see [13, 23]. However, if one is willing to change the underlying Banach space into a real interpolation space between XX and 𝒟⁡(A)\mathcal{D}(A), then the question of maximal Lq\mathrm{L}^{q}-regularity simplifies tremendously. It is a classical result of Da Prato and Grisvard [12], that is described below.

To state the result, we need to introduce the definition of a part of an operator onto another space.

Definition 2.6.

Let XX and YY be Banach spaces and C:𝒟⁡(C)⊂X→XC:\mathcal{D}(C)\subset X\to X be a linear operator. The part of CC in YY is the operator given by

𝒟⁡(𝐂):={y∈𝒟⁡(C)∩Y:C​y∈Y},𝐂​y:=C​y.\displaystyle\mathcal{D}({\bf C}):=\{y\in\mathcal{D}(C)\cap Y:Cy\in Y\},\quad{\bf C}y:=Cy.

Let in the following BB denote the time derivative operator on (0,T)(0,T), with 0<T≤∞0<T\leq\infty, i.e.,

B:{u∈W1,q​((0,T),X):u⁡(0)=0}⊂Lq​(0,T,X)→Lq​(0,T,X),u↦u′.\displaystyle B:\{u\in\mathrm{W}^{1,q}((0,T);X):u(0)=0\}\subset\mathrm{L}^{q}(0,T;X)\to\mathrm{L}^{q}(0,T;X),\quad u\mapsto u^{\prime}.

It is well-known, see, e.g., [19, Sec. 8.4-8.6], that BB is sectorial of angle π/2\pi/2.

Furthermore, let AA be a densely defined and sectorial operator of angle ω∈[0,π/2)\omega\in[0,\pi/2), i.e., −A-A is the generator of a bounded analytic semigroup. We lift the operator AA to the time-dependent space by defining

A↑:𝒟⁡(A↑):=Lq​(0,T,𝒟⁡(A))⊂Lq​(0,T,X)→Lq​(0,T,X),[A↑​u]​(t):=A​u​(t).\displaystyle A^{\uparrow}:\mathcal{D}(A^{\uparrow}):=\mathrm{L}^{q}(0,T;\mathcal{D}(A))\subset\mathrm{L}^{q}(0,T;X)\to\mathrm{L}^{q}(0,T;X),\quad[A^{\uparrow}u](t):=Au(t).

As the operator AA does not explicitly depend on time, the resolvents of A↑A^{\uparrow} and BB commute, i.e., it holds

(λ−A↑)−1​(μ−B)−1=(μ−B)−1​(λ−A↑)−1(λ∈ρ⁡(A),μ∈ρ⁡(B)).\displaystyle(\lambda-A^{\uparrow})^{-1}(\mu-B)^{-1}=(\mu-B)^{-1}(\lambda-A^{\uparrow})^{-1}\qquad(\lambda\in\rho(A),\,\mu\in\rho(B)).

In this situation, the theorem of Da Prato and Grisvard may be formulated as follows, see [12, Thm. 3.11, Lem. 3.5]:

Theorem 2.7.

Let θ∈(0,1)\theta\in(0,1) and 1≤q≤∞1\leq q\leq\infty. With the notation above, the part of the operator

C:=A↑+Bwith domain𝒟⁡(C):=𝒟⁡(A↑)∩𝒟⁡(B)\displaystyle C:=A^{\uparrow}+B\quad\textit{with domain}\quad\mathcal{D}(C):=\mathcal{D}(A^{\uparrow})\cap\mathcal{D}(B)

in the real interpolation space

(Lq​(0,T,X),𝒟⁡(A↑))θ,q=Lq​(0,T,(X,𝒟⁡(A))θ,q)\displaystyle\big(\mathrm{L}^{q}(0,T;X),\mathcal{D}(A^{\uparrow})\big)_{\theta,q}=\mathrm{L}^{q}(0,T;(X,\mathcal{D}(A))_{\theta,q})

is sectorial of angle π/2\pi/2. Furthermore, there exists M>0M>0 such that for all λ>0\lambda>0 and y∈Lq​(0,T,(X,𝒟⁡(A))θ,q)y\in\mathrm{L}^{q}(0,T;(X,\mathcal{D}(A))_{\theta,q}) it holds that A↑​(λ+A↑+B)−1​y∈Lq​(0,T,(X,𝒟⁡(A))θ,q)A^{\uparrow}(\lambda+A^{\uparrow}+B)^{-1}y\in\mathrm{L}^{q}(0,T;(X,\mathcal{D}(A))_{\theta,q}) and B​(λ+A↑+B)−1​y∈Lq​(0,T,(X,𝒟⁡(A))θ,q)B(\lambda+A^{\uparrow}+B)^{-1}y\in\mathrm{L}^{q}(0,T;(X,\mathcal{D}(A))_{\theta,q}) and that

‖A↑​(λ+A↑+B)−1​y‖Lq​(0,T,(X,𝒟⁡(A))θ,q)+‖B​(λ+A↑+B)−1​y‖Lq​(0,T,(X,𝒟⁡(A))θ,q)\hfil\displaystyle\quad\|A^{\uparrow}(\lambda+A^{\uparrow}+B)^{-1}y\|_{\mathrm{L}^{q}(0,T;(X,\mathcal{D}(A))_{\theta,q})}+\|B(\lambda+A^{\uparrow}+B)^{-1}y\|_{\mathrm{L}^{q}(0,T;(X,\mathcal{D}(A))_{\theta,q})}\hfill
≤M​‖y‖Lq​(0,T,(X,𝒟⁡(A))θ,q).\hfil\displaystyle\hfill\leq M\|y\|_{\mathrm{L}^{q}(0,T;(X,\mathcal{D}(A))_{\theta,q})}.\quad

The application of this theorem to the situation of maximal regularity is as follows. By construction, the solution operator to (2.2) is given by

(A↑+B)−1,\displaystyle(A^{\uparrow}+B)^{-1},

so that the question of whether AA has maximal Lq\mathrm{L}^{q}-regularity is about whether A↑+BA^{\uparrow}+B is invertible and whether

A↑​(A↑+B)−1andB​(A↑+B)−1\displaystyle A^{\uparrow}(A^{\uparrow}+B)^{-1}\quad\text{and}\quad B(A^{\uparrow}+B)^{-1}

are bounded. We present how to derive these properties by means of the theorem of Da Prato and Grisvard, for operators AA that are additionally invertible. Notice that the invertibility of AA implies the invertibility of A↑A^{\uparrow}. By the argument in Remark 2.5, there exists ε>0\varepsilon>0 such that A↑−εA^{\uparrow}-\varepsilon is sectorial of angle less than π/2\pi/2 as well. Applying Theorem 2.7 to C:=(A↑−ε)+BC:=(A^{\uparrow}-\varepsilon)+B shows that there exists K>0K>0 such that

‖B​(A↑+B)−1‖ℒ⁡(Lq​(0,T,(X,𝒟⁡(A))θ,q))=‖B​(ε+C)−1‖ℒ⁡(Lq​(0,T,(X,𝒟⁡(A))θ,q))≤K\displaystyle\|B(A^{\uparrow}+B)^{-1}\|_{{\mathcal{L}}(\mathrm{L}^{q}(0,T;(X,\mathcal{D}(A))_{\theta,q}))}=\|B(\varepsilon+C)^{-1}\|_{{\mathcal{L}}(\mathrm{L}^{q}(0,T;(X,\mathcal{D}(A))_{\theta,q}))}\leq K

and

∥A↑(A↑\displaystyle\|A^{\uparrow}(A^{\uparrow} +B)−1∥ℒ⁡(Lq​(0,T,(X,𝒟⁡(A))θ,q))+∥(A↑+B)−1∥ℒ⁡(Lq​(0,T,(X,𝒟⁡(A))θ,q))\displaystyle+B)^{-1}\|_{{\mathcal{L}}(\mathrm{L}^{q}(0,T;(X,\mathcal{D}(A))_{\theta,q}))}+\|(A^{\uparrow}+B)^{-1}\|_{{\mathcal{L}}(\mathrm{L}^{q}(0,T;(X,\mathcal{D}(A))_{\theta,q}))}
≤‖(A↑−ε)​(ε+C)−1‖ℒ⁡(Lq​(0,T,(X,𝒟⁡(A))θ,q))+(1+ε)​‖(ε+C)−1‖ℒ⁡(Lq​(0,T,(X,𝒟⁡(A))θ,q))\displaystyle\leq\|(A^{\uparrow}-\varepsilon)(\varepsilon+C)^{-1}\|_{{\mathcal{L}}(\mathrm{L}^{q}(0,T;(X,\mathcal{D}(A))_{\theta,q}))}+(1+\varepsilon)\|(\varepsilon+C)^{-1}\|_{{\mathcal{L}}(\mathrm{L}^{q}(0,T;(X,\mathcal{D}(A))_{\theta,q}))}
≤K.\displaystyle\leq K.

This shows that there exists a constant K>0K>0 such that whenever f∈Lq​(0,T,(X,𝒟⁡(A))θ,q)f\in\mathrm{L}^{q}(0,T;(X,\mathcal{D}(A))_{\theta,q}), the equation (2.2) has a unique solution uu satisfying

(2.3) ∥u,u′,Au∥Lq​(0,T,(X,𝒟⁡(A))θ,q)≤K∥f∥Lq​(0,T,(X,𝒟⁡(A))θ,q).\displaystyle\|u,u^{\prime},Au\|_{\mathrm{L}^{q}(0,T;(X,\mathcal{D}(A))_{\theta,q})}\leq K\|f\|_{\mathrm{L}^{q}(0,T;(X,\mathcal{D}(A))_{\theta,q})}.

In later sections, we will in particular be interested in the case q=1q=1.

We conclude this section, by shortly discussing how to extend this theory to include inhomogeneous initial values in (2.2) if q=1q=1. We have to investigate under which conditions on xx the function t↦A​T​(t)​xt\mapsto AT(t)x lies in L1​(0,T,(X,𝒟⁡(A))θ,1)\mathrm{L}^{1}(0,T;(X,\mathcal{D}(A))_{\theta,1}). Now, we use that the real interpolation space (X,𝒟⁡(A))θ,q(X,\mathcal{D}(A))_{\theta,q} can be characterized by means of the semigroup (T⁡(t))t≥0(T(t))_{t\geq 0}. Indeed, e.g., by [19, Thm. 6.2.9] it holds (in the special case 1≤q<∞1\leq q<\infty)

(2.4) (X,𝒟⁡(A))θ,q={x∈X:[x]θ,qq:=∫0∞‖t1−θ​A​T​(t)​x‖Xq​d​tt<∞}=:𝒟A​(θ,q)\displaystyle\big(X,\mathcal{D}(A)\big)_{\theta,q}=\Big\{x\in X:[x]_{\theta,q}^{q}:=\int_{0}^{\infty}\|t^{1-\theta}AT(t)x\|_{X}^{q}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}t}{t}<\infty\Big\}=:\mathcal{D}_{A}(\theta,q)

and the norms

∥x∥(X,𝒟⁡(A))θ,qand∥x∥X+[x]θ,q=:∥x∥𝒟A​(θ,q)\displaystyle\|x\|_{(X,\mathcal{D}(A))_{\theta,q}}\quad\text{and}\quad\|x\|_{X}+[x]_{\theta,q}=:\|x\|_{\mathcal{D}_{A}(\theta,q)}

are equivalent. A similar result holds for q=∞q=\infty with the obvious changes in the definition of [x]θ,q[x]_{\theta,q}. In our case q=1q=1, we directly find by the exponential decay and the analyticity of the semigroup (i.e., we use that ‖eε​s​s​A​T​(s)‖ℒ⁡(X)\|\mathrm{e}^{\varepsilon s}sAT(s)\|_{{\mathcal{L}}(X)} is uniformly bounded with respect to s>0s>0 for some ε>0\varepsilon>0) that

∫0T‖A​T​(s)​x‖X​𝑑s\displaystyle\int_{0}^{T}\|AT(s)x\|_{X}\,\mathrm{d}s ≤∫01sθ​‖s1−θ​A​T​(s)​x‖X​d​ss+∫1∞‖s​A​T​(s)​x‖X​d​ss\displaystyle\leq\int_{0}^{1}s^{\theta}\|s^{1-\theta}AT(s)x\|_{X}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}s}{s}+\int_{1}^{\infty}\|sAT(s)x\|_{X}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}s}{s}
≤∫01‖s1−θ​A​T​(s)​x‖X​d​ss+M​∫1∞e−ε​s​𝑑s​‖x‖X\displaystyle\leq\int_{0}^{1}\|s^{1-\theta}AT(s)x\|_{X}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}s}{s}+M\int_{1}^{\infty}\mathrm{e}^{-\varepsilon s}\,\mathrm{d}s\;\|x\|_{X}
≤M′​‖x‖𝒟A​(θ,1).\displaystyle\leq M^{\prime}\|x\|_{\mathcal{D}_{A}(\theta,1)}.

Moreover, using the analyticity of the semigroup again, followed by occasional applications of Fubini’s theorem and the linear substitution rule yields for some constant M>0M>0 that

∫0T∫0∞‖t1−θ​A​T​(t)​A​T​(s)​x‖X​d​tt​𝑑s\displaystyle\int_{0}^{T}\int_{0}^{\infty}\|t^{1-\theta}AT(t)AT(s)x\|_{X}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}t}{t}\,\mathrm{d}s ≤M​∫0∞∫0∞t1−θs+t​‖A​T​(12​(s+t))​x‖X​d​tt​𝑑s\displaystyle\leq M\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{t^{1-\theta}}{s+t}\|AT(\tfrac{1}{2}(s+t))x\|_{X}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}t}{t}\,\mathrm{d}s
=M​∫0∞∫t∞t1−θτ​‖A​T​(12​τ)​x‖X​𝑑τ​d​tt\displaystyle=M\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{t}^{\infty}\frac{t^{1-\theta}}{\tau}\|AT(\tfrac{1}{2}\tau)x\|_{X}\,\mathrm{d}\tau\,\frac{\mathrm{d}t}{t}
=M​∫0∞∫0τt−θ​𝑑t​‖A​T​(12​τ)​x‖X​d​ττ\displaystyle=M\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\tau}t^{-\theta}\,\mathrm{d}t\,\|AT(\tfrac{1}{2}\tau)x\|_{X}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}\tau}{\tau}
=M1−θ​∫0∞‖τ1−θ​A​T​(12​τ)​x‖X​d​ττ\displaystyle=\frac{M}{1-\theta}\int_{0}^{\infty}\|\tau^{1-\theta}AT(\tfrac{1}{2}\tau)x\|_{X}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}\tau}{\tau}
=M​21−θ1−θ​‖x‖𝒟A​(θ,1).\displaystyle=\frac{M2^{1-\theta}}{1-\theta}\|x\|_{\mathcal{D}_{A}(\theta,1)}.

Thus, for all x∈(X,𝒟⁡(A))θ,1x\in(X,\mathcal{D}(A))_{\theta,1}, we find that

∥s↦AT(s)x∥L1​(0,T,𝒟A​(θ,1))≤M∥x∥𝒟A​(θ,1).\displaystyle\|s\mapsto AT(s)x\|_{\mathrm{L}^{1}(0,T;\mathcal{D}_{A}(\theta,1))}\leq M\|x\|_{\mathcal{D}_{A}(\theta,1)}.

We formulate the results of this discussion as a corollary of the theorem of Da Prato and Grisvard.

Corollary 2.8.

Let XX be a Banach space and let −A-A be the generator of a bounded analytic semigroup on XX with 0∈ρ⁡(A)0\in\rho(A). Let θ∈(0,1)\theta\in(0,1) and 0<T≤∞0<T\leq\infty. Then for all f∈L1​(0,T,(X,𝒟⁡(A))θ,1)f\in\mathrm{L}^{1}(0,T;(X,\mathcal{D}(A))_{\theta,1}) and for all x∈(X,𝒟⁡(A))θ,1x\in(X,\mathcal{D}(A))_{\theta,1} the equation

{u′​(t)+A​u​(t)=f⁡(t)t∈(0,T),u⁡(0)=x\displaystyle\left\{\begin{aligned} u^{\prime}(t)+Au(t)&=f(t)&&t\in(0,T),\\ u(0)&=x\end{aligned}\right.

has a unique solution in the space

W1,1​((0,T),(X,𝒟⁡(A))θ,1)∩L1​(0,T,𝒟⁡(𝐀))\displaystyle\mathrm{W}^{1,1}((0,T);(X,\mathcal{D}(A))_{\theta,1})\cap\mathrm{L}^{1}(0,T;\mathcal{D}({\bf A}))

satisfying

∥u,u′,Au∥L1​(0,T,(X,𝒟⁡(A))θ,1)≤K(∥x∥(X,𝒟⁡(A))θ,1+∥f∥L1​(0,T,(X,𝒟⁡(A))θ,1)).\displaystyle\|u,u^{\prime},Au\|_{\mathrm{L}^{1}(0,T;(X,\mathcal{D}(A))_{\theta,1})}\leq K\big(\|x\|_{(X,\mathcal{D}(A))_{\theta,1}}+\|f\|_{\mathrm{L}^{1}(0,T;(X,\mathcal{D}(A))_{\theta,1})}\big).

Here, 𝐀{\bf A} denotes the part of AA on (X,𝒟⁡(A))θ,1(X,\mathcal{D}(A))_{\theta,1}.

3. Study of the Lamé operator

This section is dedicated to the study of the linearization of the velocity equation of System (1.1), when neglecting the pressure. We shall first establish various regularity results for the Lamé operator LL given by

(3.1) L=−μΔ−z∇div,L=-\mu\Delta-z\nabla\divergence,

then look at the properties of the associated semigroup, with particular attention to the maximal Lq\mathrm{L}^{q}-regularity on Besov spaces Bp,qs​(Ω,ℂd)\mathrm{B}^{s}_{p,q}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d}) up to the limit value q=1.q=1. This is done by employing Amann’s technique of inter- and extrapolation spaces. Throughout the section, Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}, d≥1d\geq 1, is a smooth bounded domain. The Lebesgue exponent pp is supposed to satisfy 1<p<∞1<p<\infty, the microlocal parameter qq satisfies 1≤q≤∞1\leq q\leq\infty, and we assume that the real number ss is such that

(3.2) −1+1p<s<1p⋅\displaystyle-1+\frac{1}{p}<s<\frac{1}{p}\cdotp

Recall that (3.2) ensures that elements of Bp,qs​(Ω,ℂd)\mathrm{B}^{s}_{p,q}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d}) have no trace at the boundary.

As a start, let us record the standard L2\mathrm{L}^{2}-theory of the Lamé operator, following the exposition in [27]. Let D​uDu denote the Jacobian matrix of a vector field u,u, and let ∇u\nabla u denote its transpose. Define the curl\curl of uu by

curl⁡u:=12​(∇u−D​u).\displaystyle\curl u:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\nabla u-Du).

Let μ>0\mu>0 and z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C} and define the sesquilinear form

(3.3) 𝔞:{W01,2​(Ω,ℂd)×W01,2​(Ω,ℂd)⟶ℂ,(u,v)⟼μ​∫Ωcurl⁡u⋅curl⁡v¯​dx+(μ+z)​∫Ωdiv⁡u​div⁡v¯​dx,\displaystyle\mathfrak{a}:\left\{\begin{aligned} \mathrm{W}^{1,2}_{0}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d})\times\mathrm{W}^{1,2}_{0}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d})&\longrightarrow\mathbb{C},\\ (u,v)\qquad&\longmapsto\mu\int_{\Omega}\curl u\cdot\overline{\curl v}\;\mathrm{d}x+(\mu+z)\int_{\Omega}\divergence u\,\overline{\divergence v}\;\mathrm{d}x,\end{aligned}\right.

where the matrix product is understood component-wise. As the complex parameter zz is not standard in usual considerations of the Lamé system, we give more details in the subsequent discussion. Under the supplementary condition that μ+Re⁡(z)>0,\mu+\operatorname{Re}(z)>0, the sesquilinear form 𝔞\mathfrak{a} is bounded and coercive, cf. [27, Lem. 3.1]. Then, define the Lamé operator on L2\mathrm{L}^{2} by

𝒟⁡(L2)\displaystyle\mathcal{D}(L_{2}) :={u∈W01,2​(Ω,ℂd):∃f∈L2​(Ω,ℂd)​ s.t. ​𝔞​(u,v)=⟨f,v⟩L2​ for all ​v∈W01,2​(Ω,ℂd)}\displaystyle:=\bigl\{u\in\mathrm{W}^{1,2}_{0}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d}):\exists f\in\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d})\text{ s.t.{} }\mathfrak{a}(u,v)=\langle f,v\rangle_{\mathrm{L}^{2}}\text{ for all }v\in\mathrm{W}^{1,2}_{0}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d})\bigr\}
L2​u\displaystyle L_{2}u :=f(u∈𝒟(L2)).\displaystyle:=f\qquad(u\in\mathcal{D}(L_{2})).

With this definition, L2L_{2} embodies (3.1) in the sense of distributions. Notice that

Cc∞​(Ω,ℂd)⊂𝒟⁡(L2)⊂W01,2​(Ω,ℂd),\mathrm{C}_{c}^{\infty}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d})\subset\mathcal{D}(L_{2})\subset\mathrm{W}^{1,2}_{0}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d}),

hence L2L_{2} is densely defined. Moreover, L2L_{2} is closed and, according to the Lax-Milgram theorem, invertible.

Following [24, Thm. 4.16 and Thm. 4.18] and using a covering argument, it is easy to obtain the following regularity result for L2L_{2} (with the convention W0,2​(Ω,ℂd)=L2​(Ω,ℂd)\mathrm{W}^{0,2}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d})=\mathrm{L}^{2}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d})).

Proposition 3.1.

Let μ>0\mu>0 and z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C} with μ+Re⁡(z)>0\mu+\operatorname{Re}(z)>0. Let k∈ℕ0k\in\mathbb{N}_{0} and Ω\Omega be a bounded domain with smooth boundary. Then, there exists a constant C>0C>0 such that for all f∈Wk,2​(Ω,ℂd)f\in\mathrm{W}^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d}) and uu given by u=L2−1​f,u=L_{2}^{-1}f, it holds

‖u‖Wk+2,2​(Ω,ℂd)≤C​‖f‖Wk,2​(Ω,ℂd).\displaystyle\|u\|_{\mathrm{W}^{k+2,2}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d})}\leq C\|f\|_{\mathrm{W}^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d})}.

Having some L2\mathrm{L}^{2}-mapping properties of the Lamé operator at our disposal, we focus now on the Lp\mathrm{L}^{p}-theory. If 2<p<∞2<p<\infty, then we define the Lamé operator on Lp​(Ω,ℂd)\mathrm{L}^{p}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d}), denoted by LpL_{p}, to be the part of L2L_{2} in Lp​(Ω,ℂd)\mathrm{L}^{p}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d}). Note that LpL_{p} is a closed operator and that Cc∞​(Ω,ℂd)\mathrm{C}_{c}^{\infty}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d}) is included in 𝒟⁡(Lp)\mathcal{D}(L_{p}).

For 1<p<21<p<2, define LpL_{p} to be the closure of L2L_{2} in Lp​(Ω,ℂd)\mathrm{L}^{p}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d}) whenever L2L_{2} is closable in this space. That L2L_{2} is indeed closable in Lp​(Ω,ℂd)\mathrm{L}^{p}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d}) is deduced by the following argument: Since L2L_{2} is closed and densely defined, its L2\mathrm{L}^{2}-adjoint L2∗L_{2}^{*} is well-defined, densely defined, and closed. Clearly, this operator is the realization of (3.1) with zz replaced by its complex conjugate z¯\overline{z}. Now, the fact that L2L_{2} is closable in Lp​(Ω,ℂd)\mathrm{L}^{p}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d}) stems from the following lemma11 1 We use the following notation and convention: the antidual space of a Banach space XX (i.e., the space of all antilinear mappings X→ℂX\to\mathbb{C}) is denoted by X′X^{\prime}. The adjoint of a densely defined operator AA is denoted by A′A^{\prime}. In the particular situation where X=Lp​(Ω,ℂd)X=\mathrm{L}^{p}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d}) and A:𝒟⁡(A)⊂Lp​(Ω,ℂd)→Lp​(Ω,ℂd)A:\mathcal{D}(A)\subset\mathrm{L}^{p}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d})\to\mathrm{L}^{p}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d}) is densely defined, the adjoint operator A′A^{\prime} is an operator A′:𝒟⁡(A′)⊂Lp​(Ω,ℂd)′→Lp​(Ω,ℂd)′A^{\prime}:\mathcal{D}(A^{\prime})\subset\mathrm{L}^{p}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d})^{\prime}\to\mathrm{L}^{p}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d})^{\prime}. The corresponding adjoint operator on Lp′​(Ω,ℂd)\mathrm{L}^{p^{\prime}}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d}) (where p′p^{\prime} stands for the Hölder conjugate exponent of pp) is denoted by A∗A^{*}. Thus, if Φ\Phi denotes the canonical isomorphism Lp′​(Ω,ℂd)→Lp′​(Ω,ℂd)′\mathrm{L}^{p^{\prime}}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d})\to\mathrm{L}^{p^{\prime}}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d})^{\prime}, then A∗A^{*} is given by (3.4) A∗:=Φ−1​A′​Φwith domain𝒟⁡(A∗):={u∈Lp′​(Ω,ℂd):Φ​u∈𝒟⁡(A′)}.\displaystyle A^{*}:=\Phi^{-1}A^{\prime}\Phi\quad\text{with domain}\quad\mathcal{D}(A^{*}):=\{u\in\mathrm{L}^{p^{\prime}}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d}):\Phi u\in\mathcal{D}(A^{\prime})\}. that can be proved by basic annihilator relations and is partly presented in [35, Lem. 2.8].

Lemma 3.2.

4. The linearized compressible Navier–Stokes system

In this section, we are concerned with the full linearized compressible Navier–Stokes system, in the case where the pressure function PP satisfies P′​(1)>0.P^{\prime}(1)>0. We strive for a maximal Lq\mathrm{L}^{q}-regularity result up to q=1q=1 on the whole time interval ℝ+.\mathbb{R}_{+}. The difficulty compared to the previous section is that we have to take into consideration the coupling between the density equation which is of hyperbolic type and the velocity equation which is of parabolic type.

As a first, let us observe that the following change of time scale and velocity:

The main steps are as follows. For completeness, let us end the section proving Theorem 1.2. As a start, we apply Theorem 4.1 with q=1q=1 and notice that the last step of the proof ensures the existence of some c>0c>0 depending only on μ,\mu, μ′\mu^{\prime} and Ω\Omega so that

To add non-zero initial data (a0,u0)∈𝒳p,1s(a_{0},u_{0})\in\mathcal{X}^{s}_{p,1} in problem (1.3) we cannot simply employ Corollary 2.8. The reason is that we would need to choose a ground space 𝒳p,1t\mathcal{X}^{t}_{p,1} for some tt slightly smaller than ss. Then we would need to calculate the real interpolation space (𝒳p,1t,𝒟⁡(Ap,1,t))θ,1(\mathcal{X}^{t}_{p,1},\mathcal{D}(A_{p,1,t}))_{\theta,1}. To circumvent this problem, consider the caloric extension

5. Global well-posedness for the compressible Navier–Stokes system

The fastest way to solve System (1.1) in the critical regularity setting is to recast it in Lagrangian coordinates. To this end, let XX be the flow associated to u,u, that is the solution to

(5.1) X⁡(t,y)=y+∫0tu⁡(τ,X⁡(τ,y))​𝑑τ.X(t,y)=y+\int_{0}^{t}u(\tau,X(\tau,y))\,\mathrm{d}\tau.

6. Local existence for general data with no vacuum

For achieving the local well-posedness of the compressible Navier–Stokes equations, there is no need to take the linear coupling of the density and velocity equations into consideration, and the sign of P′P^{\prime} does not matter. Actually, in the Lagrangian formulation (5.6), it is enough to solve the velocity equation, since Ju¯​ρ¯=ρ0J_{\bar{u}}\bar{\rho}=\rho_{0} and Ju¯J_{\bar{u}} may be computed from u¯.\bar{u}. The pressure may be seen as a source term, and combining Corollary 3.9 with s=d/p−1s=d/p-1 and q=1,q=1, with suitable nonlinear estimates allows to solve (5.6) locally in the critical regularity setting.

Clearly, a basic perturbative method relying on our reference linear system with constant coefficients is bound to fail if the density variations are too large. However, since, in our functional setting, ρ0\rho_{0} has to be uniformly continuous in Ω,\Omega, one can expect that difficulty to be challengeable if using a suitable localization argument.

Here, for expository purpose, we first present the proof of the local well-posedness in the easier case where ρ0\rho_{0} is close to some positive constant. Then, we explain what has to be modified to tackle the general case where one just assumes that it is bounded away from 0.0.

6.1. The case of small variations of density

Our goal here is to establish the following result that implies Theorem 1.1 in the case of small density variations.

Proposition 6.1.

Let the assumptions of Theorem 1.1 be in force, and assume in addition that, for a small enough α>0,\alpha>0, we have

(6.1) ‖a0‖Bp,1d/p​(Ω)≤α.\|a_{0}\|_{\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}(\Omega)}\leq\alpha.

Then, System (5.6) admits a unique solution (a¯,u¯)(\bar{a},\bar{u}) on some interval [0,T],[0,T], such that 1+a¯:=Ju¯−1​ρ01+\bar{a}:=J_{\bar{u}}^{-1}\rho_{0} is bounded away from zero on [0,T]×Ω[0,T]\times\Omega and

(a¯,u¯)∈W1,1​(0,T,Bp,1d/p​(Ω)×Bp,1d/p−1​(Ω,ℝd))∩L1​(0,T,Bp,1d/p​(Ω)×Bp,1d/p−1​(Ω,ℝd)).({\bar{a}},{\bar{u}})\in\mathrm{W}^{1,1}(0,T;\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}(\Omega)\times\mathrm{B}^{{d}/{p}-1}_{p,1}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{d}))\cap\mathrm{L}^{1}(0,T;\mathrm{B}^{{d}/{p}}_{p,1}(\Omega)\times\mathrm{B}^{d/p-1}_{p,1}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{d})).
Proof.

Throughout, we use the short notation 𝐋{\bf L} for 𝐋p,1,d/p−1.{\bf L}_{p,1,d/p-1}. Since the variations of density are small, one can look at the velocity equation as follows:

Proof of Theorem  1.1.

with λ0:=λ⁡(ρ0),\lambda_{0}:=\lambda(\rho_{0}), μ0:=μ⁡(ρ0),\mu_{0}:=\mu(\rho_{0}), 𝐋ρ0​u¯:=ρ0​∂tu¯−2​div⁡(μ0​D​(u¯))−∇(λ0​div⁡u¯){\bf L}_{\rho_{0}}{\bar{u}}:=\rho_{0}\partial_{t}{\bar{u}}-2\divergence(\mu_{0}D({\bar{u}}))-\nabla(\lambda_{0}\divergence{\bar{u}}) and ρ¯u¯:=ρ0​Ju¯−1.\bar{\rho}_{\bar{u}}:=\rho_{0}J^{-1}_{\bar{u}}.

Then, by following the proof of Proposition 6.1, it is not difficult to check that Ψ\Psi satisfies the conditions of the contraction mapping theorem on some ball B¯Fp​(T)​(uLρ0,R)\bar{B}_{\mathrm{F}_{p}(T)}(u_{L}^{\rho_{0}},R) provided RR and TT are small enough. In fact, the main changes are that the term corresponding to h¯1\bar{h}^{1} is no longer present (hence we do not need to assume ρ0\rho_{0} to be close to some constant) and that one has to bound in Bp,1d/p\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1} terms like μ⁡(ρ¯v¯)−μ0.\mu(\bar{\rho}_{\bar{v}})-\mu_{0}. However, owing to Propositions 5.2 and 5.3, and to Inequality (5.13), we may write

‖μ⁡(ρ¯v¯​(t))−μ0‖Bp,1d/p\displaystyle\|\mu(\bar{\rho}_{\bar{v}}(t))-\mu_{0}\|_{\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}} ≲‖ρ¯v¯​(t)−ρ0‖Bp,1d/p\displaystyle\lesssim\|\bar{\rho}_{\bar{v}}(t)-\rho_{0}\|_{\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}}
≲‖ρ0‖Bp,1d/p​‖Jv¯−1​(t)−1‖Bp,1d/p\displaystyle\lesssim\|\rho_{0}\|_{\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}}\|J_{\bar{v}}^{-1}(t)-1\|_{\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}}
≲‖ρ0‖Bp,1d/p​∫0t‖D​v¯‖Bp,1d/p​𝑑τ\displaystyle\lesssim\|\rho_{0}\|_{\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}}\int_{0}^{t}\|D{\bar{v}}\|_{\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}}\,\mathrm{d}\tau

hence the proof may be easily completed. The details are left to the reader. ∎

Appendix A Results on the Lamé operator

As a first, for the convenience of the reader, we recall the proof of regularity estimates in Sobolev spaces for the Lamé operator.

Proof of Proposition 3.3.

The first step is to prove that there exists a constant C>0C>0 such that all solutions u∈Wk+2,p​(Ω,ℂd)u\in\mathrm{W}^{k+2,p}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d}) to the equation

{−μΔu−z∇divu=fin ​Ωu=0on ​∂Ω\displaystyle\left\{\begin{aligned} -\mu\Delta u-z\nabla\divergence u&=f&&\text{in }\Omega\\ u&=0&&\text{on }\partial\Omega\end{aligned}\right.

for some f∈Wk,p​(Ω,ℂd)f\in\mathrm{W}^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d}) satisfy

(A.1) ∥u∥Wk+2,p​(Ω,ℂd)≤C(∥f∥Wk,p​(Ω,ℂd)+∥u∥Lp​(Ω,ℂd))⋅\|u\|_{\mathrm{W}^{k+2,p}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d})}\leq C\big(\|f\|_{\mathrm{W}^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d})}+\|u\|_{\mathrm{L}^{p}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d})}\big)\cdotp

In dimension d=1,d=1, the result readily follows by integration. In the multi-dimensional case, it is a consequence of the theory of Agmon, Douglis, and Nirenberg (more precisely [1, Thm. 10.5]). To verify the assumptions therein, define the symbol of LL by

𝒮⁡(ξ):=μ​|ξ|2​Id+z​ξ⊗ξ(ξ∈ℝd).\displaystyle\mathcal{S}(\xi):=\mu|\xi|^{2}\Id+z\xi\otimes\xi\qquad(\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{d}).
Lemma A.1.

Let μ>0\mu>0 and z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C} with μ+Re⁡(z)>0\mu+\operatorname{Re}(z)>0. Let δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) be any number that satisfies δ​μ+Re⁡(z)≥0\delta\mu+\operatorname{Re}(z)\geq 0. Then, for each ξ∈ℝd\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{d} the determinant of 𝒮⁡(ξ)\mathcal{S}(\xi) satisfies

μd​(1−δ)d​2−d2​|ξ|2​d≤|det(𝒮⁡(ξ))|≤(μ+|z|)d​|ξ|2​d.\displaystyle\mu^{d}(1-\delta)^{d}2^{-\frac{d}{2}}\lvert\xi\rvert^{2d}\leq\lvert\det(\mathcal{S}(\xi))\rvert\leq\big(\mu+\lvert z\rvert\big)^{d}\lvert\xi\rvert^{2d}.
Proof.

The result for z=0z=0 being obvious, assume from now on that z≠0.z\not=0. Let MM denote the matrix M:=ξ⊗ξM:=\xi\otimes\xi. Because MM is real and symmetric, 𝒮⁡(ξ)\mathcal{S}(\xi) is diagonalizable. Let η∈ℂd\eta\in\mathbb{C}^{d} be a unit eigenvector to 𝒮⁡(ξ)\mathcal{S}(\xi) with corresponding eigenvalue α∈ℂ\alpha\in\mathbb{C}. Then,

α​η=𝒮⁡(ξ)​η=μ​|ξ|2​η+z​M​η,hencez−1​(α−μ​|ξ|2)​η=M​η.\displaystyle\alpha\eta=\mathcal{S}(\xi)\eta=\mu\lvert\xi\rvert^{2}\eta+zM\eta,\quad\hbox{hence}\quad z^{-1}(\alpha-\mu\lvert\xi\rvert^{2})\eta=M\eta.

Hence, η\eta is an eigenvector to MM with corresponding eigenvalue z−1​(α−μ​|ξ|2)z^{-1}(\alpha-\mu\lvert\xi\rvert^{2}). Since MM is real and symmetric, η\eta and z−1​(α−μ​|ξ|2)z^{-1}(\alpha-\mu\lvert\xi\rvert^{2}) must be real. Thus, keeping in mind that |η|=1,|\eta|=1, we get

α=μ​|ξ|2+z​M​η⋅η=μ​|ξ|2+z​[ξ⋅η]2.\displaystyle\alpha=\mu\lvert\xi\rvert^{2}+zM\eta\cdot\eta=\mu\lvert\xi\rvert^{2}+z[\xi\cdot\eta]^{2}.

Let δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) be such that δ​μ+Re⁡(z)≥0\delta\mu+\operatorname{Re}(z)\geq 0 holds. This combined with μ>0\mu>0 and some trigonometry yields

|α|=|μ⁡(|ξ|2−δ​[ξ⋅η]2)+(δ​μ+z)​[ξ⋅η]2|\displaystyle\lvert\alpha\rvert=\Big\lvert\mu\big(\lvert\xi\rvert^{2}-\delta[\xi\cdot\eta]^{2}\big)+(\delta\mu+z)[\xi\cdot\eta]^{2}\Big\rvert ≥12​(μ⁡(1−δ)​|ξ|2+(δ​μ+Re⁡(z))​[ξ⋅η]2)\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\big(\mu(1-\delta)\lvert\xi\rvert^{2}+(\delta\mu+\operatorname{Re}(z))[\xi\cdot\eta]^{2}\big)
≥μ⁡(1−δ)2​|ξ|2.\displaystyle\geq\frac{\mu(1-\delta)}{\sqrt{2}}\lvert\xi\rvert^{2}.

Consequently, the determinant of 𝒮⁡(ξ)\mathcal{S}(\xi) satisfies

|det(𝒮⁡(ξ))|≥μd​(1−δ)d​2−d2​|ξ|2​d.\displaystyle\lvert\det(\mathcal{S}(\xi))\rvert\geq\mu^{d}(1-\delta)^{d}2^{-\frac{d}{2}}\lvert\xi\rvert^{2d}.

The other inequality follows from

|α|≤μ​|ξ|2+|z​[ξ⋅η]2|≤(μ+|z|)​|ξ|2.\displaystyle\lvert\alpha\rvert\leq\mu\lvert\xi\rvert^{2}+\bigl|z[\xi\cdot\eta]^{2}\bigr|\leq\big(\mu+\lvert z\rvert\big)\lvert\xi\rvert^{2}.

If d≥3d\geq 3, then Lemma A.1 implies that the operator −μΔ−z∇div-\mu\Delta-z\nabla\divergence is elliptic in the sense of Agmon, Douglis, and Nirenberg, and we get (A.1). For d=2,d=2, one needs to verify the following supplementary condition.

Lemma A.2.

Let d=2d=2 and let ξ,ξ′∈ℝ2\xi,\xi^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} be linearly independent. Then, det(𝒮⁡(ξ+τ​ξ′))\det(\mathcal{S}(\xi+\tau\xi^{\prime})) regarded as a polynomial in the complex variable τ\tau has exactly two roots with positive and two roots with negative imaginary part.

Proof.

The determinant of 𝒮⁡(ξ+τ​ξ′)\mathcal{S}(\xi+\tau\xi^{\prime}) is calculated as

(A.2) det(𝒮⁡(ξ+τ​ξ′))=μ⁡(μ+z)​[(ξ+τ​ξ′)⋅(ξ+τ​ξ′)]2.\displaystyle\det(\mathcal{S}(\xi+\tau\xi^{\prime}))=\mu(\mu+z)\big[(\xi+\tau\xi^{\prime})\cdot(\xi+\tau\xi^{\prime})\big]^{2}.

Due to the assumptions on μ\mu and zz, the prefactor cannot be zero. If there would be a real root to the equation det(𝒮⁡(ξ+τ​ξ′))=0\det(\mathcal{S}(\xi+\tau\xi^{\prime}))=0, then ξ\xi and ξ′\xi^{\prime} would have to be linearly dependent, a contradiction. Thus, (A.2) determines a fourth order polynomial in τ\tau with real coefficients and no real roots. Hence, there must be two roots with positive and with negative imaginary part. ∎

Let us now go to the existence part of the proposition. Clearly, the case p=2p=2 follows from Proposition 3.1. The case p>2p>2 will be also a consequence of it. Indeed, then LpL_{p} is injective as it is the part of L2L_{2} in Lp​(Ω,ℂd)\mathrm{L}^{p}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d}). Then by definition of the part of an operator, it holds 𝔲∈Lp′​(Ω,ℂd)′\mathfrak{u}\in\mathrm{L}^{p^{\prime}}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d})^{\prime} and (L2∗)p′∘​𝔲∈Lp′​(Ω,ℂd)′(L^{*}_{2})_{p^{\prime}}^{\circ}\mathfrak{u}\in\mathrm{L}^{p^{\prime}}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d})^{\prime}. In particular, there exists w∈Lp′​(Ω,ℂd)′w\in\mathrm{L}^{p^{\prime}}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d})^{\prime} such that for all v∈𝒟⁡((L2∗)p′)v\in\mathcal{D}((L_{2}^{*})_{p^{\prime}}) it holds

    ⟨(L2∗)p′∘​𝔲,v⟩𝒟​((L2∗)p′)′,𝒟⁡((L2∗)p′)=⟨w,v⟩(Lp′)′,Lp′.\displaystyle\langle(L^{*}_{2})_{p^{\prime}}^{\circ}\mathfrak{u},v\rangle_{\mathcal{D}((L_{2}^{*})_{p^{\prime}})^{\prime},\mathcal{D}((L_{2}^{*})_{p^{\prime}})}=\langle w,v\rangle_{(\mathrm{L}^{p^{\prime}})^{\prime},\mathrm{L}^{p^{\prime}}}.

    Consequently,

    ⟨𝔲,(L2∗)p′​v⟩(Lp′)′,Lp′=⟨(L2∗)p′∘​𝔲,v⟩𝒟​((L2∗)p′)′,𝒟⁡((L2∗)p′)=⟨w,v⟩(Lp′)′,Lp′.\displaystyle\langle\mathfrak{u},(L_{2}^{*})_{p^{\prime}}v\rangle_{(\mathrm{L}^{p^{\prime}})^{\prime},\mathrm{L}^{p^{\prime}}}=\langle(L^{*}_{2})_{p^{\prime}}^{\circ}\mathfrak{u},v\rangle_{\mathcal{D}((L_{2}^{*})_{p^{\prime}})^{\prime},\mathcal{D}((L_{2}^{*})_{p^{\prime}})}=\langle w,v\rangle_{(\mathrm{L}^{p^{\prime}})^{\prime},\mathrm{L}^{p^{\prime}}}.

    This implies that 𝔲∈𝒟⁡((L2∗)p′′)\mathfrak{u}\in\mathcal{D}((L_{2}^{*})_{p^{\prime}}^{\prime}) and that (L2∗)p′′​𝔲=w(L_{2}^{*})_{p^{\prime}}^{\prime}\mathfrak{u}=w.

    Conversely, let 𝔲∈𝒟⁡((L2∗)p′′)\mathfrak{u}\in\mathcal{D}((L_{2}^{*})_{p^{\prime}}^{\prime}). By definition, it holds 𝔲∈Lp′​(Ω,ℂd)′\mathfrak{u}\in\mathrm{L}^{p^{\prime}}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d})^{\prime} and there exists w∈Lp′​(Ω,ℂd)′w\in\mathrm{L}^{p^{\prime}}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d})^{\prime} such that for all v∈𝒟⁡((L2∗)p′)v\in\mathcal{D}((L_{2}^{*})_{p^{\prime}}) it holds

    ⟨𝔲,(L2∗)p′​v⟩(Lp′)′,Lp′=⟨w,v⟩(Lp′)′,Lp′.\displaystyle\langle\mathfrak{u},(L_{2}^{*})_{p^{\prime}}v\rangle_{(\mathrm{L}^{p^{\prime}})^{\prime},\mathrm{L}^{p^{\prime}}}=\langle w,v\rangle_{(\mathrm{L}^{p^{\prime}})^{\prime},\mathrm{L}^{p^{\prime}}}.

    Thus,

    ⟨(L2∗)p′∘​𝔲,v⟩𝒟​((L2∗)p′)′,𝒟⁡((L2∗)p′)=⟨𝔲,(L2∗)p′​v⟩(Lp′)′,Lp′=⟨w,v⟩(Lp′)′,Lp′.\displaystyle\langle(L^{*}_{2})_{p^{\prime}}^{\circ}\mathfrak{u},v\rangle_{\mathcal{D}((L_{2}^{*})_{p^{\prime}})^{\prime},\mathcal{D}((L_{2}^{*})_{p^{\prime}})}=\langle\mathfrak{u},(L_{2}^{*})_{p^{\prime}}v\rangle_{(\mathrm{L}^{p^{\prime}})^{\prime},\mathrm{L}^{p^{\prime}}}=\langle w,v\rangle_{(\mathrm{L}^{p^{\prime}})^{\prime},\mathrm{L}^{p^{\prime}}}.

    It follows that (L2∗)p′∘​𝔲∈Lp′​(Ω,ℂd)′(L^{*}_{2})_{p^{\prime}}^{\circ}\mathfrak{u}\in\mathrm{L}^{p^{\prime}}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d})^{\prime} and thus u∈𝒟⁡(𝐋p)u\in\mathcal{D}({\bf L}_{p}).

Lemma A.4.

For all 1<p<∞1<p<\infty, 1≤q≤∞1\leq q\leq\infty, and −1<s<1-1<s<1 it holds with equivalent norms that 𝒟⁡(𝐋p,q,s)=Yp,qs+1.\mathcal{D}({\bf L}_{p,q,s})=Y^{s+1}_{p,q}.

Furthermore, if θ∈(0,1)\theta\in(0,1) and s+θ<1s+\theta<1, then the part of 𝐋p,q,s{\bf L}_{p,q,s} on Xp,qs+θ≃Bp,q2​(s+θ)​(Ω,ℂd)X^{s+\theta}_{p,q}\simeq\mathrm{B}_{p,q}^{2(s+\theta)}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d}) coincides with 𝐋p,q,s+θ{\bf L}_{p,q,s+\theta}.

Proof.

First of all, recall that ℒp\mathcal{L}_{p} is invertible and that its inverse is a bounded operator

(A.5) ℒp−1:Xp−1→Xp0.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{p}^{-1}:X_{p}^{-1}\to X_{p}^{0}.

If 𝔣∈Xp1\mathfrak{f}\in X^{1}_{p}, then 𝔣\mathfrak{f} can be written as 𝔣=Φ​f\mathfrak{f}=\Phi f for some f∈𝒟⁡(Lp)f\in\mathcal{D}(L_{p}). Now, Lemma A.3 (2) implies

ℒp−1​𝔣=Φ​Lp−1​Φ−1​𝔣=Φ​Lp−1​f.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{p}^{-1}\mathfrak{f}=\Phi L_{p}^{-1}\Phi^{-1}\mathfrak{f}=\Phi L_{p}^{-1}f.

By virtue of Proposition 3.3, we thus have

‖ℒp−1​𝔣‖Xp2=‖Lp2​Lp−1​f‖Lp​(Ω,ℂd)≤C​‖Lp−1​f‖W4,p​(Ω,ℂd)≤C​‖f‖W2,p​(Ω,ℂd)≤C​‖𝔣‖Xp1.\displaystyle\|\mathcal{L}_{p}^{-1}\mathfrak{f}\|_{X^{2}_{p}}=\|L_{p}^{2}L_{p}^{-1}f\|_{\mathrm{L}^{p}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d})}\leq C\|L_{p}^{-1}f\|_{\mathrm{W}^{4,p}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d})}\leq C\|f\|_{\mathrm{W}^{2,p}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d})}\leq C\|\mathfrak{f}\|_{X^{1}_{p}}.

It follows that ℒp−1\mathcal{L}_{p}^{-1} gives rise to a bounded operator

(A.6) ℒp−1:Xp1→Xp2.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{p}^{-1}:X_{p}^{1}\to X_{p}^{2}.

Interpolating (A.5) and (A.6) reveals that for all −1<s<1-1<s<1, 1<p<∞1<p<\infty, and 1≤q≤∞1\leq q\leq\infty the operator ℒp−1\mathcal{L}_{p}^{-1} is a bounded operator

(A.7) ℒp−1:Xp,qs→Yp,qs+1.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{p}^{-1}:X^{s}_{p,q}\to Y^{s+1}_{p,q}.

Let 𝔲∈𝒟⁡(𝐋p,q,s)\mathfrak{u}\in\mathcal{D}({\bf L}_{p,q,s}). Then, by (A.7)

𝔲=ℒp−1​ℒp​𝔲∈Yp,qs+1.\displaystyle\mathfrak{u}=\mathcal{L}_{p}^{-1}\mathcal{L}_{p}\mathfrak{u}\in Y^{s+1}_{p,q}.

Moreover, since ℒp​𝔲=𝐋p,q,s​𝔲\mathcal{L}_{p}\mathfrak{u}={\bf L}_{p,q,s}\mathfrak{u}, the boundedness stated in (A.7) implies that there exists C>0C>0 such that

‖𝔲‖Yp,qs+1≤C​‖𝐋p,q,s​𝔲‖Xp,qs.\displaystyle\|\mathfrak{u}\|_{Y^{s+1}_{p,q}}\leq C\|{\bf L}_{p,q,s}\mathfrak{u}\|_{X^{s}_{p,q}}.

Conversely, let 𝔲∈Yp,qs+1\mathfrak{u}\in Y^{s+1}_{p,q}. Since 𝒟⁡(ℒp)=Lp′​(Ω,ℂd)′\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{L}_{p})=\mathrm{L}_{p^{\prime}}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d})^{\prime} and since Yp,qs+1↪Xp0=Lp′​(Ω,ℂd)′Y^{s+1}_{p,q}\hookrightarrow X^{0}_{p}=\mathrm{L}_{p^{\prime}}(\Omega;\mathbb{C}^{d})^{\prime} (cf. (3.10)), we have 𝔲∈𝒟⁡(ℒp)\mathfrak{u}\in\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{L}_{p}). By (A.7), we find ℒp​𝔲∈Xp,qs\mathcal{L}_{p}\mathfrak{u}\in X^{s}_{p,q} and the only information we need, to conclude that 𝔲∈𝒟⁡(𝐋p,q,s)\mathfrak{u}\in\mathcal{D}({\bf L}_{p,q,s}), is that 𝔲∈Xp,qs\mathfrak{u}\in X^{s}_{p,q}. This, however, follows by Proposition 3.6. Finally, the inequality follows from

‖𝐋p,q,s​𝔲‖Xp,qs=‖ℒp​𝔲‖Xp,qs≤C​‖𝔲‖Yp,qs+1.\displaystyle\|{\bf L}_{p,q,s}\mathfrak{u}\|_{X^{s}_{p,q}}=\|\mathcal{L}_{p}\mathfrak{u}\|_{X^{s}_{p,q}}\leq C\|\mathfrak{u}\|_{Y^{s+1}_{p,q}}.

Finally, to prove the second part of the lemma, we use that the domain of the part of 𝐋p,q,s{\bf L}_{p,q,s} on Xp,qs+θX^{s+\theta}_{p,q} is by definition given as

{𝔲∈𝒟(𝐋p,q,s)∩Xp,qs+θ\displaystyle\big\{\mathfrak{u}\in\mathcal{D}({\bf L}_{p,q,s})\cap X^{s+\theta}_{p,q} :𝐋p,q,s𝔲∈Xp,qs+θ}\displaystyle:{\bf L}_{p,q,s}\mathfrak{u}\in X^{s+\theta}_{p,q}\big\}
={𝔲∈𝒟⁡(ℒp)∩Xp,qs∩Xp,qs+θ:ℒp​𝔲∈Xp,qs∩Xp,qs+θ}\displaystyle=\big\{\mathfrak{u}\in\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{L}_{p})\cap X^{s}_{p,q}\cap X^{s+\theta}_{p,q}:\mathcal{L}_{p}\mathfrak{u}\in X^{s}_{p,q}\cap X^{s+\theta}_{p,q}\big\}
={𝔲∈𝒟⁡(ℒp)∩Xp,qs+θ:ℒp​𝔲∈Xp,qs+θ}\displaystyle=\big\{\mathfrak{u}\in\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{L}_{p})\cap X^{s+\theta}_{p,q}:\mathcal{L}_{p}\mathfrak{u}\in X^{s+\theta}_{p,q}\big\}
=𝒟⁡(𝐋p,q,s+θ).∎\displaystyle=\mathcal{D}({\bf L}_{p,q,s+\theta}).\qed

Appendix B Some results for Besov spaces in domains

Proof of Proposition 5.2.

Consider two real valued functions u∈Bp,1s​(Ω)u\in\mathrm{B}^{s}_{p,1}(\Omega) and v∈Bp,1d/p​(Ω).v\in\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}(\Omega). We want to prove that u​vuv lies in Bp,1s​(Ω),\mathrm{B}^{s}_{p,1}(\Omega), if −min⁡(d/p,d/p′)<s≤d/p.-\min(d/p,d/p^{\prime})<s\leq d/p. The result is classical for Ω=ℝd\Omega=\mathbb{R}^{d} and the general domain case follows from the definition of Besov spaces by restriction given in Section 3. Indeed, if u∈Bp,1s​(Ω)u\in\mathrm{B}^{s}_{p,1}(\Omega) and v∈Bp,1d/p​(Ω),v\in\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}(\Omega), then for any extension u~∈Bp,1s​(ℝd)\widetilde{u}\in\mathrm{B}^{s}_{p,1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and v~∈Bp,1d/p​(ℝd)\widetilde{v}\in\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) of uu and vv on ℝd,\mathbb{R}^{d}, we may write

‖u~​v~‖Bp,1s​(ℝd)≲‖u~‖Bp,1s​(ℝd)​‖v~‖Bp,1d/p​(ℝd).\|\widetilde{u}\,\widetilde{v}\|_{\mathrm{B}^{s}_{p,1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\lesssim\|\widetilde{u}\|_{\mathrm{B}^{s}_{p,1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\|\widetilde{v}\|_{\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}.

As u~​v~\widetilde{u}\,\widetilde{v} is an extension of u​vuv on ℝd,\mathbb{R}^{d}, taking the infimum on all extensions gives the result. ∎

Proof of Proposition 5.3.

Looking at the proof of [10, Prop. 1.7] and using the embedding of Bp,1d/p​(ℝd){\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})} in L∞​(ℝd),\mathrm{L}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), we see that in the ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} case, we do have the result with the estimate

‖K⁡(z)‖Bp,1d/p​(ℝd)≤C​(1+‖z‖Bp,1d/p​(ℝd))k​‖z‖Bp,1d/p​(ℝd)withk:=⌈d/p⌉.\|K(z)\|_{\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\leq C(1+\|z\|_{\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})})^{k}\|z\|_{\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\quad\hbox{with}\quad k:=\lceil d/p\rceil.

The result in a general domain then follows, considering all the extensions z~∈Bp,1d/p​(ℝd)\widetilde{z}\in\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) of z∈Bp,1d/p​(Ω),z\in\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}(\Omega), then taking the infimum.

The second part of the proposition follows from the first part, the following formula:

K⁡(z2)−K⁡(z1)=K′​(0)​(z2−z1)+∫01(K′​(z1+τ⁡(z2−z1))−K′​(0))​(z2−z1)​𝑑τK(z_{2})-K(z_{1})=K^{\prime}(0)(z_{2}-z_{1})+\int_{0}^{1}\bigl(K^{\prime}(z_{1}+\tau(z_{2}-z_{1}))-K^{\prime}(0)\bigr)(z_{2}-z_{1})\,\mathrm{d}\tau

and Proposition 5.2. ∎

Property (6.13) is a consequence of the following proposition.

Proposition B.1.

Let ff be in Bp,1d/p​(ℝd)\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) for some 1≤p≤∞.1\leq p\leq\infty. Let ψ\psi be a smooth function, supported in the unit ball of ℝd.\mathbb{R}^{d}. Denote ψδ,x0:=ψ(δ−1(⋅−x0))\psi_{\delta,x_{0}}:=\psi(\delta^{-1}(\cdot-x_{0})) for δ>0\delta>0 and x0∈ℝd.x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. Then,

limδ→0‖ψδ,x0​(f−f⁡(x0))‖Bp,1d/p=0uniformly with respect to ​x0.\lim_{\delta\to 0}\|\psi_{\delta,x_{0}}\>(f-f(x_{0}))\|_{\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}}=0\quad\hbox{uniformly with respect to }x_{0}.
Proof.

Let us first establish the result for gg a smooth function with bounded derivatives at all order. Let without loss of generality δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1). We first notice, owing to the mean value theorem and the fact that ψδ,x0\psi_{\delta,x_{0}} is supported in a ball of radius δ\delta that

‖∇αψδ,x0​(g−g⁡(x0))‖Lp≤C​‖∇g‖L∞​δ1+dp−αfor all ​α∈ℕ.\|\nabla^{\alpha}\psi_{\delta,x_{0}}(g-g(x_{0}))\|_{\mathrm{L}^{p}}\leq C\|\nabla g\|_{\mathrm{L}^{\infty}}\delta^{1+\frac{d}{p}-\alpha}\quad\hbox{for all }\ \alpha\in\mathbb{N}.

Next, we see that for any couple (β,γ)(\beta,\gamma) of integers with γ≥1,\gamma\geq 1,

‖∇βψδ,x0​∇γ(g−g⁡(x0))‖Lp≤C​‖∇γg‖L∞​δdp−β.\|\nabla^{\beta}\psi_{\delta,x_{0}}\>\nabla^{\gamma}(g-g(x_{0}))\|_{\mathrm{L}^{p}}\leq C\|\nabla^{\gamma}g\|_{\mathrm{L}^{\infty}}\delta^{\frac{d}{p}-\beta}.

Consequently, in light of Leibniz formula, for all integer α\alpha there exists a constant Cα>0C_{\alpha}>0 depending only on gg and such that for all x0∈ℝdx_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and δ∈(0,1),\delta\in(0,1),

‖∇α(ψδ,x0​(g−g⁡(x0)))‖Lp≤Cα​δdp+1−α.\|\nabla^{\alpha}(\psi_{\delta,x_{0}}\,(g-g(x_{0})))\|_{\mathrm{L}^{p}}\leq C_{\alpha}\delta^{\frac{d}{p}+1-\alpha}.

If α∈ℕ\alpha\in\mathbb{N} is such that d/p<α≤d/p+1d/p<\alpha\leq d/p+1, the exponent of δ\delta in the previous inequality is non-negative. Moreover, combining the derived estimates with the following interpolation inequality

‖h‖Bp,1d/p≤C​‖h‖Lp1−dp​α​‖h‖Wα,pdp​α\|h\|_{\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}}\leq C\|h\|_{\mathrm{L}^{p}}^{1-\frac{d}{p\alpha}}\|h\|_{\mathrm{W}^{\alpha,p}}^{\frac{d}{p\alpha}}

and the assumption that δ<1\delta<1 yields that there exists a constant Cg>0C_{g}>0 depending only on g,g, pp and dd such that

(B.1) ‖ψδ,x0​(g−g⁡(x0))‖Bp,1d/p≤Cg​δ(1+dp)​(1−dp​α)for all ​δ∈(0,1)andx0∈ℝd.\|\psi_{\delta,x_{0}}\,(g-g(x_{0}))\|_{\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}}\leq C_{g}\delta^{(1+\frac{d}{p})(1-\frac{d}{p\alpha})}\quad\hbox{for all }\ \delta\in(0,1)\quad\hbox{and}\quad x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Let us now prove the proposition for a general function ff in Bp,1d/p.\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}. Fix some ε>0\varepsilon>0 and take gg smooth with bounded derivatives at all order such that ‖f−g‖Bp,1d/p≤ε.\|f-g\|_{\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}}\leq\varepsilon. We have

‖ψδ,x0​(f−f⁡(x0))‖Bp,1d/p≤‖ψδ,x0​(g−g⁡(x0))‖Bp,1d/p+‖ψδ,x0​(f−g)‖Bp,1d/p+|f⁡(x0)−g⁡(x0)|​‖ψδ,x0‖Bp,1d/p.\|\psi_{\delta,x_{0}}\,(f-f(x_{0}))\|_{\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}}\leq\|\psi_{\delta,x_{0}}\,(g-g(x_{0}))\|_{\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}}+\|\psi_{\delta,x_{0}}\,(f-g)\|_{\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}}+|f(x_{0})-g(x_{0})|\|\psi_{\delta,x_{0}}\|_{\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}}.

Using Proposition 5.2, Inequality (B.1) and the embedding Bp,1d/p↪L∞,\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{L}^{\infty}, we thus have

‖ψδ,x0​(f−f⁡(x0))‖Bp,1d/p≤Cg​δ(1+dp)​(1−dp​α)+C​‖ψδ,x0‖Bp,1d/p​‖f−g‖Bp,1d/p.\|\psi_{\delta,x_{0}}\,(f-f(x_{0}))\|_{\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}}\leq C_{g}\delta^{(1+\frac{d}{p})(1-\frac{d}{p\alpha})}+C\|\psi_{\delta,x_{0}}\|_{\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}}\|f-g\|_{\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}}.

Using the invariance (up to an harmless constant) of the norm in Bp,1d/p​(ℝd)\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) by translation and dilation, and the definition of g,g, we end up with

‖ψδ,x0​(f−f⁡(x0))‖Bp,1d/p≤Cg​δ(1+dp)​(1−dp​α)+C​ε,\|\psi_{\delta,x_{0}}\,(f-f(x_{0}))\|_{\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}}\leq C_{g}\delta^{(1+\frac{d}{p})(1-\frac{d}{p\alpha})}+C\varepsilon,

which ensures

‖ψδ,x0​(f−f⁡(x0))‖Bp,1d/p≤2​C​ε\|\psi_{\delta,x_{0}}\,(f-f(x_{0}))\|_{\mathrm{B}^{d/p}_{p,1}}\leq 2C\varepsilon

provided δ\delta is small enough. ∎
